title: How Israel Camped and Marched
overview: This chapter sets out where each of Israel's twelve tribes was to camp and travel, arranged in four groups around the sacred tent at the center.

parts.label: Everyone in their place (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Each tribe was to camp together under its own flag, in a ring around the sacred tent but at some distance from it. The text never says what the flags looked like, and later Jewish tradition only guessed at animal emblems.

parts.label: Judah's group on the east (vv. 3-9)
parts.note: Judah's group, the largest, camped on the east side toward the sunrise and led the march. Judah, Issachar and Zebulun were all descended from Jacob's wife Leah, so closely related tribes stayed together.

parts.label: Reuben's group on the south (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: Reuben, the tribe of Jacob's oldest son, led the south side with Simeon and Gad and marched second. Placing Reuben behind Judah may reflect Judah's later rise as the tribe of King David, though the chapter itself gives no reason.

parts.label: The sacred tent in the middle (v. 17)
parts.note: The tent of meeting, the portable tent where God was believed to meet with Israel, camped and traveled in the very center, surrounded by the tribe of Levi. Many readers, ancient and modern, take this as picturing God at the heart of the people, much like a king's tent at the center of an army camp.

parts.label: Ephraim west, Dan north (vv. 18-31)
parts.note: Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin, all descended from Jacob's wife Rachel, held the west side. Dan, Asher and Naphtali, descended from the two servant women who bore Jacob children, held the north and brought up the rear on the march.

parts.label: The total and obedience (vv. 32-34)
parts.note: The fighting men total 603,550, matching the count in chapter 1, with the Levites left out because their work was caring for the sacred tent. The chapter closes by saying the people did exactly as instructed.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the very large numbers should be read literally, or whether the Hebrew word usually translated 'thousand' may mean a smaller clan or military unit, which would make the camp far smaller.
think: What, if anything, sits at the center of the way you arrange your life, and how did it end up there?
